document.title: The Taliban: What We've Heard
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
document.note: [Secret] Relays observations of recent visitors to Kandahar. The Taliban are well armed, militarily proficient and eager to expand to end banditry and impose Sharia. Women are ordered to stay home and male doctors are barred from treating female patients.

events.description: Visitors reported from Kandahar on Jan 22, among several recent trips there within ten days of the cable.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable compiling reports on the Taliban.
Heavy Taliban fighting in Helmand, with wounded evacuated by helicopter to Quetta.
Heavy fighting in Helmand involving Taliban; wounded evacuated by helicopter, 20 badly wounded Taliban received at ICRC hospital in Quetta.
Report from Kandahar that Taliban leaders seemed 'coached' in questions and assistance requests; fuel in Kandahar city now diesel from Pakistan rather than Iran.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable 'The Taliban: What We've Heard' sent to State Department.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable compiling reports from recent visitors to Kandahar on the Taliban's arms, funding and policies.
Taliban leaders told visitors they intend to liberate Kabul and as much of Afghanistan as possible from the commanders.
Taliban in Kandahar banned chess and marbles, imposed a three-week soccer ban that was lifted after protest, and restricted women's medical care and teaching.
The Taliban agreed to send a representative to the Mestiri mission's proposed interim governing mechanism.
Heavy fighting in Helmand involving Taliban troops; the Taliban refused visitors permission to observe it.
Taliban rehabilitated a large military compound east of Kandahar (formerly an Amir Lalai/NIFA base and a communist division HQ) and conduct artillery and tank training there.

sources_cited: BBC Pashto Service interviews with Mohammad Omar Akhund
key_claims: Visitors to Kandahar describe the Taliban as well-armed, militarily proficient and eager to expand their influence.
The Taliban claim over 4,000 paid fighters, 200 tanks, 11 MiGs and 9 transport helicopters.
Observers suspect undisclosed foreign benefactors because visible funding does not cover the Taliban's costs.
Kandahar's fuel supply shifted from Iran to Pakistan, which visitors read as sign of Pakistani support.
The Taliban recruited ex-communist officers and bureaucrats with salaries reportedly three times what commanders could pay.
The Taliban strongly oppose Iranian interference and criticize Pakistan over Malakand.
